Inductive Learning of Robot Task Knowledge from Raw Data and Online Expert Feedback

Daniele Meli Email: daniele.meli@univr.it Affiliation: Department of Computer Science    Paolo Fiorini Affiliation: Department of Engineering for Innovation Medicine, University of Verona, Strada Le Grazie 15, Verona, 37135, Italy
Abstract

The increasing level of autonomy of robots poses challenges of trust and social acceptance, especially in human-robot interaction scenarios. This requires an interpretable implementation of robotic cognitive capabilities, possibly based on formal methods as logics for the definition of task specifications. However, prior knowledge is often unavailable in complex realistic scenarios.

In this paper, we propose an offline algorithm based on inductive logic programming from noisy examples to extract task specifications (i.e., action preconditions, constraints and effects) directly from raw data of few heterogeneous (i.e., not repetitive) robotic executions. Our algorithm leverages on the output of any unsupervised action identification algorithm from video-kinematic recordings. Combining it with the definition of very basic, almost task-agnostic, commonsense concepts about the environment, which contribute to the interpretability of our methodology, we are able to learn logical axioms encoding preconditions of actions, as well as their effects in the event calculus paradigm.

Since the quality of learned specifications depends mainly on the accuracy of the action identification algorithm, we also propose an online framework for incremental refinement of task knowledge from user’s feedback, guaranteeing safe execution.

Results in a standard manipulation task and benchmark for user training in the safety-critical surgical robotic scenario, show the robustness, data- and time-efficiency of our methodology, with promising results towards the scalability in more complex domains.

keywords
Inductive Logic Programming, Answer Set Programming, Learning Under Uncertainty, Online Learning, Human-Robot Interaction, Explainable AI

1 Introduction

Robots are becoming increasingly popular in many fields of industry and society. As their degree of autonomy, hence intelligence, increases, human-robot interaction is a crucial aspect of design in the development of robotic systems, to preserve human safety and increase social acceptance in complex, typically human-centered scenarios. In this context, recent international provisions and regulations, e.g., by the European Union11 1 Artificial Intelligence Act, https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/TA-9-2023-0236_EN.html prescribe interpretability (Rosenfeld and Richardson, 2019) as one fundamental requirement to achieve safe and transparent human-robot interaction. To this aim, formal representation of agents’ (robots’) environments and tasks is a suitable and convenient choice. Such representations in robotics include, among others, action languages for planning (Erdem and Patoglu, 2012), as the well-established Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) by Haslum et al (2019); Estivill-Castro and Ferrer-Mestres (2013); Kootbally et al (2015), logic programming for plan re-configuration (Meli et al, 2023b), ontology-based systems (Manzoor et al, 2021) and behavior trees (Ögren and Sprague, 2022). One fundamental limitation of these approaches is the assumption of full scenario and task knowledge, which is clearly impractical in complex, uncertain or partially observable domains.

In this paper, we propose a methodology to derive logical task specifications from visual and kinematic data of robotic executions. In particular, we assume prior knowledge of very basic commonsense concepts (features) about the environment, e.g., related to relative positions of objects in the scene. These are usually shared among many tasks and scenarios, and they are already encoded in available general-purpose ontologies for robotic and automation, e.g., by Schlenoff et al (2012). We then combine automatic retrieval of environmental features from input execution data, with unsupervised action identification. The resulting matching examples of action execution and environmental features are used in an Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) by Muggleton and De Raedt (1994) framework to derive salient task specifications, namely, preconditions and effects of actions and constraints. Learned specifications are affected by the noise in the input data and their post-processing (i.e., environmental features retrieval and unsupervised action identification), thus they may not immediately applied for safe fully autonomous robotic planning and execution. Hence, we finally propose a framework interleaving human and autonomous execution, allowing for incremental knowledge refinement via robot teaching.

This paper then makes the following contributions:

  • •

    we propose ILP under the semantics of Answer Set Programming (ASP) by Lifschitz (2019) to learn task specifications from little noisy raw data of robotic execution. Our methodology can work in combination with any action identification algorithm, exploiting the output of the latter to define noise in action examples, and is robust . Moreover, following our previous work in Meli et al (2021a), we employ the representation of event calculus (Mueller, 2008) to efficiently learn temporal specifications about environmental features, i.e., effects of actions;

  • •

    we propose an ILP- and ASP-based framework for time- and data-efficient incremental learning of task knowledge and autonomous robotic planning, involving an expert human in the loop to guarantee safe execution. The proposed framework represents an extension of our preliminary work in Meli et al (2023a), where we did not learn effects of actions and showcased only a simple example of precondition refinement for one action, without evaluating the performance quantitatively for the full task;

  • •

    we evaluate our approach with different action identification algorithms and with a partial ablation study (considering or neglecting unobserved action examples). We operate in the domain of surgical task automation, specifically in the benchmark peg transfer scenario from the Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery (FLS) in Soper and Fried (2008), using da Vinci robot and Research Kit (dVRK) (Kazanzides et al, 2014). Broadly speaking, the surgical scenario poses fundamental challenges in the field of task knowledge retrieval, e.g., the scarce availability of data due to legal and organisational issues, and the paramount importance of safety and social acceptance, thus justifying the use of data-efficient and interpretable learning with ILP. With particular reference to the peg transfer scenario, it is one of the most challenging tasks from FLS, which must be accomplished in the smallest time and with the highest number of successful repetitions22 2 https://www.flsprogram.org/technical-skills-training-curriculum/. Indeed, the peg transfer requires dual arm coordination and reasoning on the placements of rings and pegs, which stresses the mental focus and resistance of the surgeon under time constraints in a real operating room. Moreover, this task is not only paradigmatic in the clinical context, but it is also an example of a generic structured robotic pick-and-place task. Thus, our experiments are designed to show promising results towards the general applicability of our methodology to more general robotic and automation domains;

  • •

    we make publicly available the code for replicating experimental results and the framework for incremental task knowledge refinement33 3 https://github.com/danm11694/ILASP_robotics.git.

In the following, we first revise state of the art in robotic task learning, in Section 2. Then, in Section 3 we provide relevant background about the fundamental components of our framework, ASP and ILP, as well as a description of the peg transfer task useful as a leading example. Finally, we detail our methodology in Section 4, perform experimental validation in Section 5 and draw conclusions with limitations and future perspectives in Sections 6-7.

2 Related Works

Learning robotic task sequences from previous observations or human teaching is a widely studied problem, especially in the area of industrial assembly and manipulation (Zhu and Hu, 2018; Mukherjee et al, 2022). State-of-the-art approaches rely on probabilistic models to capture the variability of the environment and execution, e.g., Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) as in Calinon (2016); Kyrarini et al (2019) and Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) as in Tanwani and Calinon (2016); Medina and Billard (2017).

With the recent uptake of deep learning and large data models, neural architectures have been employed both for online and offline learning of optimal robotic strategies for complex domains. Main approaches involve reward shaping to learn efficient task policies from human demonstrations (Alakuijala et al, 2023), or end-to-end learning of sensor-action maps for robotic navigation (Liu et al, 2017) and manipulation (Rahmatizadeh et al, 2018). This has paved the way towards human-in-the-loop Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), where humans communicate with the autonomous robot either to show it safe and best practice under different situations (Huang et al, 2024), acting as teachers (Shenfeld et al, 2023), or to give targets and commands, based on pre-trained foundational visual-language models (Shah et al, 2023).

In the specific field of robotic surgery, HMMs have been used, e.g., by Berthet-Rayne et al (2016), though more general Bayesian networks are the most popular (Blum et al, 2008; Charrière et al, 2017). Recently, DRL is becoming a prominent approach to surgical task automation (Shahkoo and Abin, 2023; Fan et al, 2024; Corsi et al, 2023), paving the way towards interactive human-robot learning (Long et al, 2023).

One crucial limitation, especially for DRL and deep learning methods, is their scarce interpretability and the lack of safety guarantees, even when safe (Shahkoo and Abin, 2023) or human-in-the-loop (Huang et al, 2024) solutions are employed. Indeed, these approaches heavily rely on large and diverse training datasets, failing at the generalization to similar but different task situations. For this reason, some researchers have attempted to directly learn human models of agency (Nikolaidis et al, 2015; Chen et al, 2020), which however severely limit the performance of the autonomous agent. Similar limitations hold for Bayeesian and statistical methods. As an example in the surgical setting, 80 homogeneous (i.e., under the same environmental conditions) executions are required by Berthet-Rayne et al (2016) to learn a HMM for a good replication of the yet relatively simple peg transfer task. Finally, these approaches are highly sensitive to parameter initialization, as shown by Medina and Billard (2017).

In contrast, in this paper we propose to use ILP (Muggleton, 1991) to learn task specifications, i.e., preconditions, effects and constraints on actions; and then perform automated reasoning in on specifications in ASP formalism for task planning and execution. Originated from the broad field of domain knowledge discovery (Sridharan and Meadows, 2018; Mota and Sridharan, 2020; Laird et al, 2017), ILP solves many limitations of above machine learning and DRL approaches, being data- and time-efficient, and able to easily generalize theory from data. Furthermore, the interpretable logical formalism allows easier interaction with humans for online task knowledge refinement. For this reason, ILP has been successfully applied to robotic learning (Cropper and Muggleton, 2019; Meli et al, 2020; Meli et al, 2021a).

However, one important limitation of ILP, and in general frameworks for high-level knowledge extraction, is the poor performance in the presence of noisy datasets, i.e., task examples with uncertainty. For this reason, researchers have tried to embed uncertainty into the inductive process, as Katzouris et al (2023) to learn event definitions and Law (2023) under the more generic answer set semantics. In this direction, neurosymbolic approaches have been proposed, e.g., differentiable inductive logic programming (Evans and Grefenstette, 2018; Shindo et al, 2021) and statistical relational learning (Marra et al, 2024; Hazra and De Raedt, 2023), which however suffer from scalability issues and cannot be currently applied out of toy robotic domains, unless strict task-specific constraints are imposed to the ILP problem (Hazra and De Raedt, 2023). For instance, we tried to apply the publicly available code released by Evans and Grefenstette (2018) to the peg transfer domain, but it failed for the large space of possible specifications to be learned.

Under the framework of ILP in the ASP semantics, we stem from our previous works on fully supervised task specifications learning in Meli et al (2020); Meli et al (2021a), considering the more realistic use case of ILP examples generated from an unsupervised action identification algorithm applied on raw robotic execution data. We then extend Meli et al (2023a) to refine task knowledge (including effects of actions) from human feedback via online ILP, guaranteeing safe execution thanks to expert supervision. We use the state-of-the-art ILASP (Inductive Learning of Answer Set Programs) tool by Law (2018) for its theoretical and empirical advantages against main competitors as Katzouris et al (2016); Schüller and Benz (2018); Cropper and Morel (2021), encompassing learning from noisy data, context-dependent examples (capturing the action-environment connection particularly relevant in robotic tasks) and the possibility to induce most probable ASP theories, i.e., covering most of the examples. Moreover, the answer set semantics supported by ILASP is the state of the art for planning (Erdem et al, 2016), especially in robotic contexts (Erdem and Patoglu, 2018; Meli et al, 2023b).

3 Background and notation

In this section, we describe the paradigmatic peg transfer task, to use it as a leading example in the rest of the paper. We then provide basic notions about ASP and ILP under the ASP semantics, necessary to detail our methodology next.

We start by providing a list of relevant symbols used throughout the paper, as a practical reference to the reader.

3.2 The peg transfer task

Figure 1 shows the setup for the illustrative surgical training task of peg transfer. The objective is to place colored rings on pegs of the corresponding color using the two patient-side manipulators (PSM1 and PSM2) of the dVRK. Each PSM can grasp any reachable ring and place it on any reachable peg; reachability is determined by the relative position of rings and pegs with respect to the center of the base. Reachability regions are identified by the red dashed line in Figure 1. For instance, PSM1 can reach the red ring and the blue peg, while PSM2 can reach the blue ring and the green peg. In case an arm can reach a ring but not the same-colored peg, it must move to the center of the base and transfer the ring to the other arm to complete the task. Pegs can be occupied by other rings and must be freed before placing the desired ring on it. Also, rings may be on pegs or on the base in the initial state, i.e., some rings may need to be extracted before being moved.

3.3 ASP planning task description

We describe the peg transfer task in an established format for Answer Set Programming (ASP) by Calimeri et al (2020).

A (planning) domain’s description in ASP comprises a sorted signature and axioms. The sorted signature is the alphabet of the domain, defining constants (either Booleans, strings or integers), variables and atoms, i.e., predicates of variables. In the peg transfer domain, variables represent arms A (with constant value either psm1 or psm2), objects O (either ring or peg) and colors (either red, green, blue, yellow or grey). Atoms represent concepts as the relative locations between objects and / or arms (e.g., at(A,ring,C), meaning that arm A is at the location of ring with color C, or placed(ring,C1,peg,C2), meaning that ring with color C1 is placed on peg with color C2) and the status of grippers of arms (e.g., closed_gripper(A). In our previous work (Meli et al, 2021a) we considered more task-specific environmental concepts, e.g., in_hand(A,R,C) to represent that a ring is held by an arm. However, these can be derived from other atoms (for instance, in_hand(A,R,C) holds when both at(A,R,C) and closed_gripper(A) do), so we omit them in this paper, in order to allow dependency only on basic kinematic information from the robot and preserve generalization to different tasks. Atoms also represent actions of the task, i.e., move(A,O,C) (moving to a colored ring or peg), move(A,center,C) (moving to center for transfer of ring C), grasp(A,ring,C), release(A) and extract(A,ring,C) for gripper actions and extraction, respectively. We further annotate atoms with a temporal variable t representing the discrete time step of the task flow (e.g., move(A,O,C,t)). Whenever all variables in an atom are assigned with constant values, we say that the atom is ground.

Given the sorted signature, axioms define preconditions and effects of actions and constraints. Preconditions for the peg transfer task (in the form Action : Precondition) are:

0 {move(A, O, C, t) : reachable(A, O, C, t); (1a)
move(A, center, C, t) : at(A, R, C, t), closed_gripper(A, t); (1b)
extract(A, ring, C, t) : at(A, ring, C, t), closed_gripper(A, t); (1c)
grasp(A, ring, C, t) : at(A, ring, C, t); (1d)
release(A, t) : at(A, ring, C, t), closed_gripper(A, t)} 1. (1e)

where the aggregate construct 0 {..} 1 indicates that only one action per time step can be executed, given that the corresponding precondition holds.

Effects of actions are expressed according to the generic paradigm of event calculus by Kowalski and Sergot (1989), i.e., a generic environmental atom F is subject to the law of inertia:

holds(F, t) :- initiated(F, t).
holds(F, t) :- holds(F, t-1), not terminated(F, t).

where :- equals to ←\leftarrow (logical implication) and not is the default negation (if a Boolean bb is not known to be true, i.e., unobserved, then not bb is true). The inertia law can be interpreted as follows: an environmental atom starts holding as some initiated(F) condition holds, and ends holding at the occurrency of some terminated(F) condition. As an example, consider the peg transfer task. Atom at(A,ring,C) starts holding when move(A,ring,C) has been executed, and terminates only when arm A moves away. The inertia law is valid in every robotic scenario involving interaction with the environment. Effects of actions in the peg transfer task are then equivalently described by the following initiating and terminating conditions:

initiated(closed_gripper(A), t) :- grasp(A, ring, C, t-1). (2a)
initiated(placed(ring, C1, peg, C2), t) :- at(A, ring, C1, t-1),
     closed_gripper(A, t-1), at(A, peg, C2, t-1), release(A, t-1). (2b)
initiated(at(A, ring, C), t) :- move(A, ring, C, t-1). (2c)
initiated(at(A, peg, C), t) :- move(A, peg, C, t-1). (2d)
initiated(at(A, center), t) :- move(A, center, C, t-1). (2e)
terminated(closed_gripper(A), t) :- release(A, t-1). (2f)
terminated(placed(ring, C1, peg, C2), t) :- extract(A, ring, C1, t-1),
    color(C2). (2g)
terminated(at(A, ring, C1), t) :- move(A, ring, C2, t-1), color(C1). (2h)
terminated(at(A, ring, C1), t) :- move(A, peg, C2, t-1), color(C1). (2i)
terminated(at(A, ring, C1), t) :- move(A, center, C2, t-1), color(C1). (2j)
terminated(at(A, peg, C1), t) :- move(A, peg, C2, t-1), color(C1). (2k)
terminated(at(A, peg, C1), t) :- move(A, ring, C2, t-1), color(C1). (2l)
terminated(at(A, peg, C1), t) :- move(A, center, C2, t-1), color(C1). (2m)
terminated(at(A, center), t) :- move(A, O, C, t-1). (2n)

The specification of color(C2) in axioms (2g)-(2m) is required in ASP to guarantee safety of rules, i.e., all variables on the left-hand side (head of rule) of logical implication must appear without negation on the right-hand side (body of rule).

Finally, constraints of the task are:

:- move(A, center, C1, t), closed_gripper(A, t), at(A, ring, C2, t),
     placed(ring, C2, peg, C3, t). (3a)
:- move(A, peg, C1, t), closed_gripper(A, t), at(A, ring, C2, t),
     placed(ring, C2, peg, C3, t). (3b)
:- move(A, ring, C, t), closed_gripper(A, t). (3c)
:- move(A, peg, C1, t), placed(ring, C2, peg, C1, t). (3d)

The lack of head atoms is equivalent to ⊥←…\bot\leftarrow\ldots, i.e., body atoms cannot concurrently be ground, otherwise falsum ⊥\bot would be implied. The semantics of above constraints is then, respectively: arm A1 cannot move to the center for transfer if it is holding a ring which is still placed on a peg (extraction is required); arm A1 cannot move to a peg if it is holding a ring which is still placed on a peg; an arm with closed gripper cannot move to a ring; an arm cannot move to an occupied peg.

Given the task description, an ASP solver computes (possibly multiple) answer sets, i.e., the minimal sets of ground atoms satisfying the specifications. Each answer set contains actions to be executed at each time step, and the corresponding environmental context.

3.4 Inductive learning of ASP theories

We now provide relevant definitions to introduce the problem of inductive learning of ASP theories in our considered scenario. Additional details can be found in Law et al (2018).

A generic ILP problem T\pazocal{T} for ASP theories is defined as the tuple T=⟨B,SM,E⟩\pazocal{T}=\langle B,S_{M},E\rangle, where BB is the background knowledge, i.e. a set of axioms and atoms in ASP syntax; SMS_{M} is the search space, i.e. the set of candidate ASP axioms that can be learned; and EE is a set of examples. The goal of T\pazocal{T} is to find a subset H⊆SMH\subseteq S_{M} such that H∪B⊧EH\cup B\models E. In ILASP (Law, 2018) tool considered in this paper, examples are partial interpretations defined as follows.

Definition 1 (Partial interpretation).

Let PP be an ASP program. Any set of ground atoms that can be generated from axioms in PP is an interpretation of PP. Given an interpretation II of PP, we say that a pair of subsets of grounded atoms e=⟨ei​n​c,ee​x​c⟩e=\langle e^{inc},e^{exc}\rangle (respectively the included and excluded set) is a partial interpretation (extended by interpretation II) if ei​n​c⊆Ie^{inc}\subseteq I and ee​x​c∩I=∅e^{exc}\cap I=\emptyset.

In particular, we consider context-dependent partial interpretations, as introduced by Law et al (2016).

Definition 2 (Context-dependent partial interpretation (CDPI)).

A CDPI of an ASP program P with an interpretation I is a tuple ec=⟨e,C⟩e_{c}=\langle e,C\rangle, where ee is a partial interpretation and CC is an ASP program called context. II is said to extend ece_{c} if ei​n​c∪C⊆Ie^{inc}\cup C\subseteq I and (ee​x​c∪C)∩I=∅(e^{exc}\cup C)\cap I=\emptyset.

To better understand CDPIs, consider the task of learning preconditions of action release(A,t) in the peg transfer domain. Hence, SMS_{M} includes axioms in the form release(A,t) :- F1, …Fn, being Fi a generic environmental atom of the task. In ILASP syntax, a CDPI may be expressed as

#pos(id, {release(psm1,1)}, {release(psm2,1)}, {at(psm1,peg,red,1), (4)
    closed_gripper(psm1,1), closed_gripper(psm2,1), …}).

where id denotes the unique identifier of the example, ei​n​c={release(psm1,1)}e^{inc}=\{{\small\texttt{release(psm1,1)}}\} means that the gripper of PSM1 was open at time step 1, ee​x​c={release(psm2,1)}e^{exc}=\{{\small\texttt{release(psm2,1)}}\} means that the gripper of PSM2 was not open at time step 1, and C={at(psm1,ring,red,1),…}C=\{{\small\texttt{at(psm1,ring,red,1)}},\ldots\} is the set of ground environmental atoms at time step 1. In other words, ei​n​ce^{inc} and ee​x​ce^{exc} include the ground atoms corresponding to the head of the axioms to be learned, while CC includes all other ground atoms.

We now specialize T\pazocal{T} to CDPIs as follows:

Definition 3 (Learning ASP theories from CDPIs).

An ILASP learning task from CDPIs is a tuple T=⟨B,SM,E⟩\pazocal{T}=\langle B,S_{M},E\rangle, where EE is a set of CDPIs. We say that H⊆SMH\subseteq S_{M} is a solution to T\pazocal{T} if the following holds:

∀e∈E​∃A​S​s.t.B∪H∪C⊧A​S:e​ is extended by ​A​S\forall e\in E\ \exists AS\ s.t.\ B\cup H\cup C\models AS:\ e\textrm{ is extended by }AS

More specifically, ILASP computes the shortest hypothesis, i.e., the one with minimal number of atoms.

For instance, from example (4), ILASP can learn

release(A, t) :- at(A, peg, C, t). (5)

where the excluded set of example (4) allows to discard the possible axiom release(A, t) :- closed_gripper(A, t).

In this paper, we consider an extension of the task in Definition 3, i.e., learning ASP theories from noisy CDPIs as proposed by Law (2018):

Definition 4 (Learning ASP theories from noisy CDPIs).

An ILASP learning task from noisy CDPIs is a tuple T=⟨B,SM,E⟩\pazocal{T}=\langle B,S_{M},E\rangle, where EE is a set of NN noisy CDPIs, i.e., CDPIs annotated with an integer weight wi,∀i=1​…​Nw_{i},\forall i=1\ldots N. We say that H⊆SMH\subseteq S_{M} is a solution to T\pazocal{T} if the following holds:

∀e∈E​∃A​S​s.t.B∪H∪C⊧A​S:e​ is extended by ​A​S\forall e\in E\ \exists AS\ s.t.\ B\cup H\cup C\models AS:\ e\textrm{ is extended by }AS (6)

More specifically, ILASP computes the hypothesis which minimizes the cost Γ=λ+η\Gamma=\lambda+\eta, where λ\lambda is the number of atoms in the axioms of the hypothesis and η=∑i=1Kwiu\eta=\sum_{i=1}^{K}w^{u}_{i}, being {wiu}i=1K\{w^{u}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K} the set of weights for K≤NK\leq N uncovered examples, i.e., CDPIs not satisfying axiom (6).

In other words, Definition 4 introduces the possibility to “ignore” some examples, if their weight is low. This is particularly useful to discard highly uncertain examples, e.g., resulting from poor-quality identification. Consider, for instance, the following noisy CDPIs:

#pos(id@​1​, {release(psm1,1)}, {release(psm2,1)}, {at(psm1,peg,red,1), \displaystyle{\small\texttt{\#pos(id@}}1{\small\texttt{, \lx@text@lbrace release(psm1,1)\lx@text@rbrace, \lx@text@lbrace release(psm2,1)\lx@text@rbrace, \lx@text@lbrace at(psm1,peg,red,1), }}
    closed_gripper(psm1,1), closed_gripper(psm2,1), …}). (7a)
#pos(id@​2​, {release(psm1,3)}, {release(psm2,3)}, {at(psm1,peg,red,3), \displaystyle{\small\texttt{\#pos(id@}}2{\small\texttt{, \lx@text@lbrace release(psm1,3)\lx@text@rbrace, \lx@text@lbrace release(psm2,3)\lx@text@rbrace, \lx@text@lbrace at(psm1,peg,red,3), }}
    at(psm2,peg,blue,3), closed_gripper(psm1,3), …}). (7b)

The first one would lead to learn

release(A, t) :- at(A, peg, C, t). (8)

while from the second one

release(A, t) :- closed_gripper(A, t). (9)

However, axiom (9) has Γ=2+1=3\Gamma=2+1=3 (CDPI (7a) is not covered), while axiom (8) has Γ=2+2=4\Gamma=2+2=4 (CDPI (7b) is not covered). For this reason, ILASP selects (8) as the best hypothesis.

Finally, we consider another extension to Definition 3, including negative examples as in Sakama and Inoue (2009).

Definition 5 (Learning ASP theories from positive and negative CDPIs).

Consider An ILASP learning task T=⟨B,SM,E⟩\pazocal{T}=\langle B,S_{M},E\rangle as in Definition 3, where E=⟨E+,E−⟩E=\langle E^{+},E^{-}\rangle is a set of CDPIs split into two sub-sets E+,E−E^{+},E^{-}, with the latter being negative and the former positive examples. We say that H⊆SMH\subseteq S_{M} is a solution to T\pazocal{T} if the following holds:

∀e∈E+​∃A​S​s.t.B∪H∪C⊧A​S:e​ is extended by ​A​S\displaystyle\forall e\in E^{+}\ \exists AS\ s.t.\ B\cup H\cup C\models AS:\ e\textrm{ is extended by }AS
∀e∈E−​∄​A​S​s.t.B∪H∪C⊧A​S:e​ is extended by ​A​S\displaystyle\forall e\in E^{-}\ \nexists AS\ s.t.\ B\cup H\cup C\models AS:\ e\textrm{ is extended by }AS

In other words, while standard positive examples describe allowed (but not mandatory) ground atoms to be modeled by the learned ASP theory, negative examples are more strong and describe forbidden ground atoms, hence typically leading to the learning of task constraints. For instance, from example (4) ILASP may learn either axiom (5) or:

0 { release(A, t) : closed_gripper(A, t)} 1. (10)

since the aggregate construct implies that release(A, t) may or may not be grounded, thus ei​n​c={release(psm1, 1)},ee​x​c={release(psm2, 1)}e^{inc}=\{{\small\texttt{release(psm1, 1)}}\},e^{exc}=\{{\small\texttt{release(psm2, 1)}}\} are still allowed by Definition 3. However, if we add to example (4) the negative example:

#neg(id, {release(psm2,1)}, {)}, {at(psm1,peg,red,1),
    closed_gripper(psm1,1), closed_gripper(psm2,1), …}).

axiom (10) is not allowed from Definition 5, since it could still model ei​n​c={release(psm2, 1)}e^{inc}=\{{\small\texttt{release(psm2, 1)}}\} which is now strictly forbidden.

4 Methodology

In this section, we present our methodology for unsupervised learning and online supervised refinement of ASP task knowledge.

4.1 Unsupervised learning of ASP task knowledge

The unsupervised learning strategy is sketched in Algorithm 1. More specifically, in Section 4.1.1 we describe how to generate the action-context tuples, starting from a dataset of synchronized visual and kinematic executions of the task. Then, in Section 4.1.3 and 4.1.4, we show how to build examples from action-context tuples, in order to learn ASP axioms for constrained preconditions, and how to generate axioms for effects of actions in the event calculus, respectively. While explaining different components of our strategy, we refer to specific lines in Algorithm 1.

4.1.1 Action-context tuples generation

The input to our learning pipeline is a dataset SS of execution traces, i.e. synchronized kinematic and video streams of an instance of the task. Recording assumes that the robot and the vision system share a common reference frame, e.g., using the calibration procedure by Roberti et al (2020).

The kinematic stream includes the following features K\pazocal{K}: i) Cartesian coordinates of each arm AA of the robotic system 𝐩A={xp​o​s,A,yp​o​s,A,zp​o​s,A}\mathbf{p}_{A}=\{x_{pos,A},y_{pos,A},z_{pos,A}\}; ii) quaternion coordinates of each arm AA of the robotic system 𝐪A={xo​r,A,yo​r,A,zo​r,A,wo​r,A}\mathbf{q}_{A}=\{x_{or,A},y_{or,A},z_{or,A},w_{or,A}\}; iii) opening angles jAj_{A} of the grippers. Other works by van Amsterdam et al (2019); Despinoy et al (2015) consider additional kinematic features, e.g., Cartesian and rotational velocities; however, following our previous work (Meli and Fiorini, 2021), we decide not to consider them without loss of generality.

The video stream is acquired from a RGBD camera. The following geometric features G\pazocal{G} are extracted using standard color segmentation and shape recognition with random sample consensus (Fischler and Bolles, 1981): i) center position 𝐩r​c={xr​c,yr​c,zr​c}\mathbf{p}_{rc}=\{x_{rc},y_{rc},z_{rc}\} of each ring with color cc; ii) tip position 𝐩p​c={xp​c,yp​c,zp​c}\mathbf{p}_{pc}=\{x_{pc},y_{pc},z_{pc}\} of each peg with color cc; iii) position 𝐩b={xb,yb,zb}\mathbf{p}_{b}=\{x_{b},y_{b},z_{b}\} of meeting point at the center of the base for transfer; iv) ring radius r​rrr.

Kinematic and visual geometric quantities can be automatically mapped to environmental features F\pazocal{F} at each time step with the following relations, as proposed by Ginesi et al (2020):

at(A,ring,C) ←‖𝐩A−𝐩r​c‖2<r​r\displaystyle\leftarrow||\mathbf{p}_{A}-\mathbf{p}_{rc}||_{2}<rr (11)
at(A,peg,C) ←‖𝐩A−𝐩p​c‖2<r​r∧zp​c<zp​o​s,A\displaystyle\leftarrow||\mathbf{p}_{A}-\mathbf{p}_{pc}||_{2}<rr\ \land\ z_{pc}<z_{pos,A}
placed(ring,C1,peg,C2) ←‖𝐩r​c​1−𝐩p​c​2‖2<r​r∧zr​c​1<zp​c​2\displaystyle\leftarrow||\mathbf{p}_{rc1}-\mathbf{p}_{pc2}||_{2}<rr\ \land\ z_{rc1}<z_{pc2}
reachable(A,O,C) ←a​r​g​m​i​nA​|yo​c−yp​o​s,A|=A\displaystyle\leftarrow argmin_{A}|y_{oc}-y_{pos,A}|=A
closed_gripper(A) ←jA<π8\displaystyle\leftarrow j_{A}<\frac{\pi}{8}
at(A,center) ←‖{xp​o​s,A,yp​o​s,A}−{xb,yb}‖2<r​r\displaystyle\leftarrow||\{x_{pos,A},y_{pos,A}\}-\{x_{b},y_{b}\}||_{2}<rr
44footnotetext: yo​cy_{oc} denotes the yy-coordinate of entity O∈\in{ring, peg}.55footnotetext: π8\frac{\pi}{8} is chosen empirically to identify that the gripper is closed, since the angle is not exactly 00 from the encoders of dVRK.

The set F\pazocal{F} in this paper includes only commonsense information about the relative position of objects and robotic arms and the status of the gripper, hence discarding higher-level concepts as the arm is holding a ring defined by Meli and Fiorini (2021). In this way, we reduce the amount of sophisticated prior knowledge required for action identification and task knowledge induction. In fact, the definition of semantic features may be retrieved or straightforwardly derived from available domain ontologies, e.g., by Gibaud et al (2018) for surgery and Schlenoff et al (2012) for robotics and automation (for instance, relative positions are connected to the concept of distance, retrieved from the already available PositionPoint class in Schlenoff et al (2012)), thus requiring minimal effort from the human designer.

We can now generate the action-context tuples needed for our learning pipeline, using any algorithm Φ\Phi for action identification from video-kinematic input. Such algorithms split the visual-kinematic stream of execution into NN timed segments ⟨Ki,Gi,ti⟩\langle\pazocal{K}_{i},\pazocal{G}_{i},t_{i}\rangle (Line 4), where Ki\pazocal{K}_{i} and Gi\pazocal{G}_{i} are respectively the kinematic and geometric features for the specific segment starting at tit_{i}. Then, they cluster similar segments according to a distance metric di​j:Ki×Gi×Kj×Gj→ℝ+d_{ij}:\pazocal{K}_{i}\times\pazocal{G}_{i}\times\pazocal{K}_{j}\times\pazocal{G}_{j}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{+}.

We then convert each ii-th timed segment to |L||\pazocal{L}| action-context tuples (set P\pazocal{P}) ⟨lj,Ci,ρi​j⟩,∀j=1,…,|L|\langle l_{j},C_{i},\rho_{ij}\rangle,\\ \forall j=1,\ldots,|\pazocal{L}| (Line 6), where CiC_{i} is the context set G⁡(F)G(\pazocal{F}) of ground environmental features computed from Ki\pazocal{K}_{i} and Gi\pazocal{G}_{i} via relations (11); ljl_{j} is the unique identifier of an abstract (non-ground) action of the task in the set L\pazocal{L}; ρi​j∈[0,1]\rho_{ij}\in[0,1] is the confidence level of the tuple, defined as:

ρi​j=1−di​j∑k=1|L|di​k\rho_{ij}=1-\frac{d_{ij}}{\sum\limits_{k=1}^{|\pazocal{L}|}d_{ik}}

In other words, the action-context tuple states that under the context CiC_{i}, an action of type ljl_{j} has been executed with probability ρi​j\rho_{ij}.

In this paper, we assume that the number of actions in L\pazocal{L}, i.e., |L||\pazocal{L}|, is known in advance. It is reasonable, since typically the set of allowed actions of a robotic task (hence their corresponding motion primitives) is assumed as known (Kim et al, 2021; Goel and Brunskill, 2019), e.g., provided directly in the annotations of the benchmark JIGSAWS dataset for surgical gestures analysis (Gao et al, 2014). On the contrary, semantic information as the target of an action (e.g., move(A, ring, C) has a ring with color C as a target), its effects and preconditions are not known and must be discovered from the execution traces. As a consequence, while the actual set of abstract action for peg transfer should be L=\pazocal{L}={move(A,ring,C), move(A,peg,C), move(A,center,C), release(A), grasp(A,ring,C), extract(A, ring, C)}, we only consider a less informative set L={lj(A)},∀j=1,…,|L|\pazocal{L}=\{l_{j}(\pazocal{A})\},\forall j=1,\ldots,|\pazocal{L}|. where A\pazocal{A} is a subset of the available robotic arms (|A|≤2|\pazocal{A}|\leq 2 in peg transfer) actually involved in the specific action execution. The set A\pazocal{A} can be easily retrieved from the kinematic features, e.g., evaluating the variation of 𝐩A\mathbf{p}_{A} and 𝐪A\mathbf{q}_{A} from the beginning to the end of each timed segment returned from the identification algorithm.

4.1.2 Constraints as extended action preconditions

The ILASP formulation considered for unsupervised task knowledge learning reflects Definition 4, i.e., excluding negative examples. Though it is possible to define noisy negative examples and extend Definition 5 similarly to Definition 4, this would not be a correct modeling approach. In fact, we learn task knowledge from examples generated by an unsupervised action identification algorithm, which only considers observed executions of specific actions, without any information about not executed actions. Hence, similarly to our previous works on discovering procedural knowledge from uncertain execution (Mazzi et al, 2023b; Meli et al, 2024), our task mainly matches the definition of positive examples with an included (observed) and and excluded (unobserved) set in the CDPIs, rather than introducing strictly forbidding negative examples.

At the same time, only negative examples allow to learn hard constraints typical of real robotic tasks. For this reason, we embed constraints as extended preconditions of actions. In fact, constraints (3a)-(3d) can be added to preconditions (1) as:

0 {move(A,ring,C,t) : reachable(A,ring,C,t),not closed_gripper(A,t); (12a)
move(A,peg,C,t) : reachable(A,peg,C,t),not placed(ring,C1,peg,C,t); (12b)
move(A,peg,C,t) : reachable(A,peg,C,t), not placed(ring,C1,peg,C2,t),
    closed_gripper(A,t),at(A,ring,C1,t); (12c)
move(A,center,C,t) : at(A,ring,C,t),not placed(ring,C,peg,C1,t),
    closed_gripper(A,t),at(A,ring,C1,t); (12d)
extract(A,ring,C,t) : at(A,ring,C,t),closed_gripper(A,t); (12e)
grasp(A,ring,C,t) : at(A,ring,C,t); (12f)
release(A,t) : at(A,ring,C,t),closed_gripper(A,t)} 1. (12g)

where constraint (3a) is embedded in axiom (12d), constraints (3b)-(3d) are represented in (12b)-(12c) and constraint (3c) is added to precondition (12a).

4.1.3 Learning extended action preconditions

We now show how to translate action-context tuples into CDPIs for learning ASP task knowledge. We assume that axioms for each action can be learned separately, i.e., it is possible to launch ILP tasks in Definition 4 in parallel for all actions. This is reasonable, since we want to capture ASP axioms matching partial interpretations to the context, i.e., relations between actions and environmental features similar to the ones presented in Section 3.3. Hence, mutual dependencies between actions can be ignored, since they are implicitly represented with effects of actions on the environmental context. Moreover, we discard ii-th action-context tuple for a given action label lj (Lines 9-10) if

ρi​j<1N​∑k=1Nρk​j\rho_{ij}<\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\rho_{kj} (13)

In this way, we reduce the input noise to ILASP.

For each i,ji,j-th action-context tuple, we then build a noisy CDPI (Line 18) in the form:

#pos(id@​ρi​j​, ​G​(lj)​, ​H​(lj)∖G⁡(lj)​, ​Ci​).{\small\texttt{\#pos(id@}}\rho_{ij}{\small\texttt{, }}G(l_{j}){\small\texttt{, }}\pazocal{H}(l_{j})\setminus G(l_{j}){\small\texttt{, }}C_{i}{\small\texttt{).}} (14)

where H⁡(lj)\pazocal{H}(l_{j}) is the Herbrand base of lj=lj​(A)l_{j}=l_{j}(\pazocal{A}), i.e., the set of all possible ground atoms which can be derived from ljl_{j} (i.e., the different possible assignments of arm variables in A\pazocal{A}); G⁡(lj)⊆H⁡(lj)G(l_{j})\subseteq\pazocal{H}(l_{j}) is the set of ground atoms actually observed at the specific time step represented by the example. For instance, if PSM1 moves towards the red ring, ljl_{j} corresponds to move(A, ring, C) = ljl_{j}(A), G(lj)={ljG(l_{j})=\{l_{j}(psm1)}, H(lj)={lj\pazocal{H}(l_{j})=\{l_{j}(psm1), ljl_{j}(psm2)}. The set ee​x​ce^{exc} allows to learn extended preconditions embedding constraints.

Given these CDPIs, for each ljl_{j} we define an ILASP task (Line 19) to learn extended action preconditions (set X\pazocal{X}), with background knowledge containing the definition of F\pazocal{F} and ASP variables (see Section 3.3) and the search space consisting of axioms in the form ljl_{j} :- F1,…{}_{1},\ldots, Fn, being Fi∈F,∀i=1,…,n{}_{i}\in\pazocal{F},\forall i=1,\ldots,n.

4.1.4 Generating effects of actions

The quality of axioms representing effects of actions depends on the accuracy in the identification of action labels. We generate axioms corresponding to effects of actions as follows. Assuming the i,ji,j-th action-context tuple represents the task situation at timestep tt, with context Ct≡CiC_{t}\equiv C_{i}, we evaluate the differences between Ct−1C_{t-1}-CtC_{t} on one side, and Ct+1C_{t+1}-CtC_{t} on the other side66 6 In Algorithm 1, we denote the temporal subscript as ii in the definition of the contexts (Lines 12-16). In fact, from Line 5 and Line 8, i∈1,…,Ni\in 1,\ldots,N. On the contrary, in the main text of the paper, we use t−1t-1 and t+1t+1 to refer to previous and following temporal instants, since we assume some action-context tuples have already been removed by criterion (13), hence the sequence of ii’s does not necessarily match the temporal sequence.. Specifically, for each ground atom f∈G⁡(F){\small\texttt{f}}\in G({\small\texttt{F}}), with F∈F\in\pazocal{F}, we verify:

  • •

    if f∈Ct\in C_{t} and f∉Ct−1\notin C_{t-1}, we define a probabilistic initiating example ⟨F,lj,ρi​j⟩\langle{\small\texttt{F}},l_{j},\rho_{ij}\rangle, meaning that the effect of ljl_{j} is to ground the environmental atom F with probability ρi​j\rho_{ij} (Lines 13-14);

  • •

    if f∈Ct\in C_{t} and f∉Ct+1\notin C_{t+1}, we define a probabilistic terminating example ⟨F,lj,ρi​j⟩\langle{\small\texttt{F}},l_{j},\rho_{ij}\rangle, meaning that the effect of ljl_{j} is to unground the environmental atom F with probability ρi​j\rho_{ij} (Lines 15-16).

For each F, we obtain a set of probabilistic initiating and terminating examples IF\pazocal{I}_{{\small\texttt{F}}}, EF\pazocal{E}_{{\small\texttt{F}}}, respectively. We then rank these sets according to

ρ¯j=1K​∑i=1Kρi​j∀⟨F,lj,ρi​j⟩∈IF​(respectively,EF)\bar{\rho}_{j}=\frac{1}{K}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{K}\rho_{ij}\quad\forall\langle{\small\texttt{F}},l_{j},\rho_{ij}\rangle\in\pazocal{I}_{{\small\texttt{F}}}\ (\mathrm{respectively,}\ \pazocal{E}_{{\small\texttt{F}}})

The above mean measures the accuracy of identifying a generic action ljl_{j} as an initiating or terminating condition for a semantic feature F. We then identify ljel_{j}^{e} and ljil_{j}^{i}, corresponding respectively to maxρ¯j⁡EF\max_{\bar{\rho}_{j}}\pazocal{E}_{{\small\texttt{F}}} and maxρ¯j⁡IF\max_{\bar{\rho}_{j}}\pazocal{I}_{{\small\texttt{F}}} (Lines 22-23). We finally define the following starting and ending conditions for F (Lines 24-25):

initiated(F, t) :- lji.\displaystyle{\small\texttt{initiated(F, t) :- }}l_{j}^{i}.
terminated(F, t) :- lje.\displaystyle{\small\texttt{terminated(F, t) :- }}l_{j}^{e}.

whose collection constitutes the sets I,E\pazocal{I},\pazocal{E} of initiating and terminating conditions, respectively, describine the effects of robotic actions on the environment.

4.2 Online supervised refinement of ASP task knowledge

Learned preconditions X\pazocal{X} and initiating / terminating conditions (I\pazocal{I} / E\pazocal{E}) for effects of actions may be incomplete or inexact, depending on the quality of the input video-kinematic stream SS and the accuracy of the chosen unsupervised action identification algorithm Φ\Phi. Hence, especially in safety-critical scenarios as robotic surgery, we must design a shared autonomy framework where autonomous ASP reasoning (based on learned task knowledge) is interleaved with human control. At the same time, shared autonomy is useful to continuously improve the autonomous system, exploiting human feedback as a teacher.

Two main assumptions underlie our methodology: i) ASP action labels are directly mapped to motion primitives for actual robotic execution; ii) a perception system (in our case, a RGB-D camera and kinematic sensors from the robot) is available to automatically ground semantic features F\pazocal{F} and perform reasoning. Both are reasonable. In fact, once timed segments are clustered according to action labels, it is possible to efficiently learn in closed form the corresponding primitive for each action, e.g., as shown by Ginesi et al (2020); Ginesi et al (2021b). Moreover, semantic features are simple geometric re-interpretations of kinematic and geometric features from sensors, according to relations (11), and Ginesi et al (2020); Tagliabue et al (2022); Meli et al (2021b) showed that they can be efficiently computed for online planning.

We now detail the main steps of our proposed methodology. First, preconditions in X\pazocal{X} are converted to a set of aggregate preconditions Xa\pazocal{X}_{a}:

0 {l0: F1,F2,…,Fn;\displaystyle{\small\texttt{0 \lx@text@lbrace}}l_{0}{\small\texttt{: F}}_{1},{\small\texttt{F}}_{2},\ldots,{\small\texttt{F}}_{n}; (15)
l1: F1,F2,…,Fn;\displaystyle\ \ \ \ l_{1}{\small\texttt{: F}}_{1},{\small\texttt{F}}_{2},\ldots,{\small\texttt{F}}_{n};
…\displaystyle\ \ \ \ \ldots
l|L|: F1,F2,…,Fn} 1.\displaystyle\ \ \ \ l_{|\pazocal{L}|}{\small\texttt{: F}}_{1},{\small\texttt{F}}_{2},\ldots,{\small\texttt{F}}_{n}{\small\texttt{\lx@text@rbrace 1.}}

where Fi∈F,∀i=1,…,n{}_{i}\in\pazocal{F},\forall i=1,\ldots,n. In this way, we set up an ASP program combining E,I,Xa\pazocal{E},\pazocal{I},\pazocal{X}_{a} which can be used for online task planning.

At the beginning of the task, the perception system grounds semantic features, thus triggering ASP reasoning. The generated plan is a sequence of actions Sa=⟨a1,a2,…,an⟩S_{a}=\langle{\small\texttt{a}}_{1},{\small\texttt{a}}_{2},\ldots,{\small\texttt{a}}_{n}\rangle, selected for execution according to a FIFO policy. Before executing a1{\small\texttt{a}}_{1}, which is an instance of some ljl_{j}, the user is asked a feedback on whether he approves it or not. In case of approval, we generate and store a positive not noisy CDPI for ljl_{j}:

#pos(id,{a1},H⁡(lj)∖{a1},Ct​).{\small\texttt{\#pos(id}},\{{\small\texttt{a}}_{1}\},\pazocal{H}(l_{j})\setminus\{{\small\texttt{a}}_{1}\},C_{t}{\small\texttt{).}}

being CtC_{t} the set of ground environmental features at current time tt perceived by sensors. Otherwise, we generate and store a negative not noisy example:

#neg(id,{a1},{},Ct​).{\small\texttt{\#neg(id}},\{{\small\texttt{a}}_{1}\},\{\},C_{t}{\small\texttt{).}}

We then ask the user for a feasible action au{\small\texttt{a}}_{u}, which is an instance of, e.g., li,i≠jl_{i},i\neq j, and store a positive CDPI:

#pos(id,{au},H⁡(li)∖{au},Ct​).{\small\texttt{\#pos(id}},\{{\small\texttt{a}}_{u}\},\pazocal{H}(l_{i})\setminus\{{\small\texttt{a}}_{u}\},C_{t}{\small\texttt{).}}

Then, we execute an action a∗{\small\texttt{a}}^{*} (either au{\small\texttt{a}}_{u} or aj{\small\texttt{a}}_{j}), transiting to time step t+1t+1. At this point, we evaluate each ground environmental feature f occurring in CtC_{t} but not in Ct+1C_{t+1} (respectively, viceversa), and generate a positive CDPI for terminating (respectively, initiating) conditions of F = G−1G^{-1}(f) (i.e., the corresponding not ground semantic feature) as:

#pos(id, {terminated(f, t+1)}, {}, ​Ct∖{f}∪{a∗}​).\displaystyle{\small\texttt{\#pos(id, \lx@text@lbrace terminated(f, t+1)\lx@text@rbrace, \lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace, }}C_{t}\setminus{\small\texttt{\lx@text@lbrace f\lx@text@rbrace}}\cup\{{\small\texttt{a}}^{*}\}{\small\texttt{).}}
respectively
#pos(id, {initiated(f, t+1)}, {}, ​Ct∖{f}∪{a∗}​).\displaystyle{\small\texttt{\#pos(id, \lx@text@lbrace initiated(f, t+1)\lx@text@rbrace, \lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace, }}C_{t}\setminus{\small\texttt{\lx@text@lbrace f\lx@text@rbrace}}\cup\{{\small\texttt{a}}^{*}\}{\small\texttt{).}}

After an action belonging to ljl_{j} has been forbidden, and an alternative one belonging to lil_{i} has been provided by the user, we run ILASP online for both action labels, as well as the initiating and terminating conditions for all newly grounded or ungrounded semantic features. We then update corresponding axioms in E,I,Xa\pazocal{E},\pazocal{I},\pazocal{X}_{a}. In this way, we do not refine task knowledge at each step of execution, which would be too computationally demanding, but only when the autonomous system exhibits unwanted, potentially unsafe behavior (i.e., available task knowledge is not correct).

5 Results

We now validate our methodology in the peg transfer domain. Specifically, we first analyze the performance of Algorithm 1 on a relatively small dataset containing both visual and kinematic information about task execution. Then, we show how to practically include learned task knowledge into an autonomous robotic framework as the one by Ginesi et al (2020), in order to realize shared autonomy with incremental refinement of ASP task knowledge.

All experiments are run on a computer with AMD Ryzen 7 3700x CPU (8 cores, 16 threads, 4.4 GHz4.4\text{\,}\mathrm{G}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z} nominal frequency) and 32 GB32\text{\,}\mathrm{G}\mathrm{B} RAM.

5.1 Unsupervised learning of ASP task knowledge

We generate an input video-kinematic stream SS for Algorithm 1, from the three task instances depicted in Figure 2, executed by a user in teleoperation with dVRK and using Intel Realsense RGB-D camera for visual acquisition. In Figure 2(a), the task starts in the nominal situation described in FLS (Soper and Fried, 2008), with all 4 colored rings placed on grey pegs, on the opposite side with respect to the corresponding pegs. Hence, PSMs must perform transfer before placing rings on pegs. In Figure 2(b), a more challenging situation is depicted. Relevant rings and pegs (i.e., the blue and red ones) are on one side of the peg base, hence no transfer is needed. However, rings occupy pegs with mismatched color, thus one of the colored peg must be freed (by placing a ring on a grey peg temporarily), before completing the task. Figure 2(c) shows an unconventional scenario with the red ring on the same side as its peg, while the blue ring is on the opposite side out of any peg. Hence, not all rings require extraction in this task instance. Furthermore, before placing the blue ring on its peg (hence, after transfer), the ring fell, hence it had to be grasped again to complete the task. These three task examples well represent different flows of executions of peg transfer. However, their major challenge lies in the fact that actions are not equally represented. For instance, move(A, center, C) occurs only 5 times (4 times in Figure 2(a) and once in Figure 2(c)), while release(A) occurs 21 times (10 times in Figure 2(a), 5 times in Figure 2(b) and 6 times in Figure 2(c)).

We evaluate the performance of Algorithm 1 in terms of standard precision, recall and F1-score achieved by learned axioms, given a random environmental context for the task. We assess the performance of the algorithm when using different unsupervised action identification strategies Φ\Phi. In particular, we consider our methodology proposed in Meli and Fiorini (2021) and the original work by Despinoy et al (2015), achieving lower F1-score, especially on small heterogeneous datasets of executions (as the one in Figure 2). We refer the reader to the two references for more details. The essential difference between Meli and Fiorini (2021) and Despinoy et al (2015) is that the latter only consider the kinematic signature to cluster action segments, while the former also take into account the environmental representation given by the semantic features. Hence, Meli and Fiorini (2021) are more robust to heterogeneous motions (a peculiarity of our dataset). For this reason, from now on we refer to the variant with the algorithm by Despinoy et al (2015) as Ak​i​nA_{kin}, while the variant with the algorithm by Meli and Fiorini (2021) as As​e​mA_{sem}. Moreover, we also consider a baseline version of our algorithm where we perform action identification as in Meli and Fiorini (2021) and do not consider the excluded set in CDPIs of equation (14). In other words, we learn task knowledge only from observed examples of execution, neglecting counterexamples which lead to discovering constraints (extended action preconditions). We expect the performace to degrade with the accuracy of the underlying action identification strategy.

In order to evaluate learned axioms for extended action preconditions by each algorithm version, we generate 1000 random contexts (i.e., ground semantic environmental features) for the task. For each context, we then compute feasible ground actions (only one time step ahead in the future, hence immediate actions implied by the context), performing ASP reasoning on both handcrafted task knowledge (Section 3.3) and learned axioms. Whenever the latter match the implications of the former, a true positive (T​PTP) is counted. Otherwise, a false positive (F​PFP) is considered. We thus compute precision, recall and F1-score as:

P​r=T​PT​P+F​P​R​e​c=T​PT​P+F​N​F​1=2​P​r⋅R​e​cP​r+R​e​cPr=\frac{TP}{TP+FP}\hfill Rec=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}\hfill F1=2\frac{Pr\cdot Rec}{Pr+Rec}

To evaluate learned effects of actions, we perform analogous experiments, but considering 1000 random action-context pairs, i.e., the same random contexts as above paired with one possible action each. In all tests, we also randomize the number of reachable rings ∈{1,2,3,4}\in\{1,2,3,4\}.

For axioms related to actions, ILASP is run setting a maximum length of axioms up to 6 (i.e., 1 head atom and up to 5 body atoms), resulting in ≈10200\approx 10200 axioms in the search space per action (learning tasks for actions are run in parallel, since they are mutually independent). As outlined in Algorithm 1, effects of actions are not learned via ILASP.

We report the learned axioms with the three considered algorithms in Appendix 8.1. Learning times in Table 1 show that the baseline algorithm is the fastest one, since only executed actions are presented to ILASP, thus the tool does not take into account extended action preconditions (constraints on actions), resulting in simpler yet more incomplete task knowledge. Algorithm As​e​mA_{sem} requires less time than Ak​i​nA_{kin}. In fact, the latter have a lower action identification accuracy, thus examples are more noisy and ILASP converges more slowly to a final hypothesis. The only exception is for move(A, ring, C), which is learned within 4 s4\text{\,}\mathrm{s} when using Despinoy et al (2015). However, in this case ILASP actually finds the empty hypothesis. For this reason, in Appendix 8.1.2 we introduce the trivial axiom:

move(A, ring, C, t) :- arm(A), color(C).

meaning that moving to a ring is always possible.

Table 2 shows the quantitative results regarding the quality of learned axioms. For each metric, we report median and Inter-Quartile Range (IQR). We highlight the best results in bold (we focus first on the highest median, then on the lowest IQR). When using As​e​mA_{sem}, the F1-score is the highest in most cases. When evaluating effects of actions (statistics about initiating and terminating conditions are merged), the baseline algorithm achieves the same performance as As​e​mA_{sem}. In fact, as explained in Section 4.1.4, the excluded set introduced in CDPIs in equation (14) for learning action preconditions does not affect the way we learn axioms for effects. Thus, the main element affecting the results for effects of actions is the chosen unsupervised action identification algorithm. The baseline algorithm achieves the worst performance at learning action preconditions for grasping, releasing and extracting. In fact, these actions involve repetitive fast motions, either opening / closing of the gripper or a simple motion normal to the peg base. On the contrary, in our non-homogeneous dataset, moving actions correspond to different shapes of motion, depending on the specific locations of rings and pegs. Thus, the kinematic signature of action segments is more heterogeneous and induces higher errors in Despinoy et al (2015). For this reason, the baseline algorithm still achieves better results than Ak​i​nA_{kin}.

5.2 Online supervised refinement of ASP task knowledge

Learned axioms from Algorithm 1 may be incomplete and unsafe for practical application in a fully autonomous robotic framework, due to inaccuracies of unsupervised action identification and Algorithm 1 itself. We now show how our shared autonomy framework (Section 4.2) can be applied to ensure safety and realize incremental refinement of learned ASP task knowledge, embedding (expert) human feedback in the reasoning and execution loop. In particular, we investigate how precision, recall and F1-score of axioms evolve, as they are refined through expert feedback during the execution of the task (for fair comparison, we do not consider the aggregate transformation in equation 15, i.e., we consider all possible ground atoms from learned axioms).

We use a simulated model of the peg transfer scenario with dVRK and a RGB-D sensor77 7 Calibration between the PSMs and the camera is assumed as a prior, achieved, e.g., via the methodology proposed by Roberti et al (2020)., based on the Robot Operating System88 8 https://ros.org and built in CoppeliaSim environment99 9 https://www.coppeliarobotics.com/ and shown in Figure 3. As explained in Section 4.2, we assume that motion primitives for each action class are preliminarily learned from clusters generated from the unsupervised action identification algorithm by Meli and Fiorini (2021), using, e.g., dynamic movement primitives proposed by Ginesi et al (2020)1010 10 An user may also specify a motion primitive for each action, e.g., a trivial linear interpolation between starting and goal position. In any case, we focus only on task-level learning and refinement, thus motion learning is out of the scope of this paper..

We start from learned axioms with As​e​mA_{sem}. In fact, the methodology explained in Section 4.2 is not affected by the specific action identification algorithm.

We execute the autonomous framework in the three ordered scenarios depicted in Figure 3. The scene in Figure 3(a) shows a specific task situation with rings to be placed on pegs without transfer. Transferring is however required for rings in Figure 3(b). Finally, Figure 3(c) depicts a slightly more challenging scenario with occupied pegs. Thus, the sequence of selected scenarios, while relatively short (42 total actions, fewer than the training dataset used in Section 5.1), requires progressive task knowledge refinement and encodes main variants of peg transfer.

Table 3 shows the quantitative analysis on the rules learned after the three simulated scenarios were completed (the final task knowledge is reported in Appendix 8.2). Bold entries indicate an improved F1-score at the end of execution, meaning that learned axioms are more accurate. In general, the average F1-score increases from 88%88\% to 93%93\%, i.e., overall task knowledge is refined. Axioms for actions improve or maintain the same performance achieved from offline learning. For effects of actions, at(A, ring, C) achieves lower performance. A closer look at finally learned axioms for the corresponding initiating conditions, in equations (16k)-(16l), the atoms starts to be ground when either move(A, ring, C) action is executed, or the arm which cannot reach the peg moves to center for transfer (in this case, in fact, the other arm reaches the ring at the transfer location). These initiating conditions are complete for the atom, and extend the only partial knowledge encoded in the original axioms learned offline (Appendix 8.1.1). However, the terminating conditions in equations (16i)-(16j) only respectively specify that at(A, ring, C) stops holding when, at transfer location, the other arm moves to the peg to place the ring, or the ring is released on a peg. Compared with ground-truth axioms in equations (2h)-(2j), these terminating conditions are still incomplete, since at(A, ring, C) should stop holding whenever A moves away. Collecting examples for all such occurrencies would require more task iterations and variants. Moreover, these considerations hold for all atoms representing the current location of arms, thus justifying the slightly worse performance achieved for at(A, peg, C) (higher IQR). The median improvement on at(A, center), instead, rises from the scarce examples for move(A, center, C) in the dataset for offline learning (only 4 instances in scenarios depicted in Figure 2). Thus, while the results for the action do not vary after online ASP refinement, the results for its effect improve.

ILASP was called 13 times, i.e., ≈30%\approx 30\% times over all required actions to complete the task instances. We remark that each time ILASP was invoked, the user voted the autonomous-generated action as invalid, hence not correct and useful (in the best case) or potentially unsafe. This demonstrates the fundamental role of our knowledge refinement architecture for autonomy implementation.

From a computational perspective, the median - IQR required time for running ILASP was 2.81 s2.81\text{\,}\mathrm{s} - 6.07 s6.07\text{\,}\mathrm{s}1111 11 The search space is the same as for offline learning., thus compatible with practical application of our framework to real robotic scenarios with non-strict real-time requirements. Moreover, the computational performance may be optimized by using the more efficient FastLAS extension to ILASP by Law et al (2020). However, this aspect is out of the scope of this paper, which is more methodological.

6 Discussion

Our experiments evidence the efficacy of our methodology for offline robotic task knowledge learning from raw data, and interactive online refinement via human feedback.

Thanks to the generalization capabilities of logical task formalization, offline learning via ILP is highly data- and time-efficient, and robust to non-homogeneous small datasets of executions (i.e., non-repetitive action sequences under diverse environmental conditions), regardless of the specific action identification algorithm. Moreover, our framework for online incremental learning from expert feedback is time-efficient, allowing to easily refine task knowledge online, thanks to the interpretable interface provided by ASP formalism to the human expert. Since the human can forbid unwanted actions and a deterministic logical task theory is progressively refined, the overall task execution is guaranteed to be safe, neglecting human fallacies.

This work opens to several research problems and opportunities for improvement, as outlined in the following.

Prior knowledge of actions and environmental features

We make the assumption that all possible task actions and environmental features, i.e., the ASP signature of the task, are known in advance (though the environmental features are almost task-agnostic, since they only describe relative positions of entities of the task). In more complex robotic scenarios, involving, e.g., multiple robots with different capabilities (as in industrial robotics or real clinical setups), this may be infeasible.

A possible solution is to learn relevant task concepts from available textbooks, if available. For instance, in the context of robotic surgery, pre-trained transformers have been employed by Bombieri et al (2023b); Bombieri et al (2024) to automatically retrieve relevant surgical concepts from natural language. However, real robotic scenarios may still present novel unseen flows of execution, where the system must be able to learn about new actions and new environmental features. For such cases, we plan to extend our framework to support new concept learning, which requires some modifications to the current software architecture.

Advanced symbol grounding

Given the complete signature of the ASP task, we rely on standard image and kinematic segmentation techniques to retrieve grounded symbols, following Rules (11). In more complex tasks with multiple sensor inputs, more sophisticated situation awareness may be required.

To this aim, in the future we plan to investigate the use of advanced symbol grounding techniques (Topan et al, 2021), recently applied to the problem of DRL under temporal logic specifications (Umili et al, 2023).

Task and motion learning

An impelling requirement from the robotic research community is to jointly learn high-level routines and low-level motion strategies (James et al, 2020). This can be achieved with hierarchical learning architectures (Sridharan et al, 2019), or exploiting curriculum-based human demonstrations (Huang et al, 2024). However, these cannot be applied to hazardous scenarios as surgical robotics, where fast, safe and efficient learning is required from few examples. For this reason, we will integrate online one-shot imitation learning with dynamic movement primitives (Ginesi et al, 2019; Ginesi et al, 2021a), to work simultaneously with the task-level ILP pipeline.

Bottom-up vs. top-down learning

Our approach to task knowledge learning is bottom-up, i.e., it starts from raw data of robotic executions. Another approach to retrieve domain knowledge involves natural language processing applied to manuals and expert annotations, as shown, e.g., by Bombieri et al (2023a); Pan et al (2023); Fuggitti and Chakraborti (2023). In the future, we plan to combine the two methodologies, exploiting background knowledge extracted from domain-specific texts in the offline and online learning processes.

Probabilistic task knowledge

At the moment we learn deterministic task specifications, accounting for uncertainty only when defining examples and covering the most of them accordingly (see Defintion 4). However, as shown, e.g., by Berthet-Rayne et al (2016), a more accurate task representation may be provided by probabilistic logical specifications. Learning probabilistic logical theories has been already explored, e.g., in the event calculus formalism by Katzouris and Artikis (2020). Alternatively, statistical relational learning by Hazra and De Raedt (2023); Marra et al (2024) retrieves probabilistic knowledge graphs, but presents significant computational limitations for its applicability to complex robotic scenarios and online learning.

In the future, we plan to investigate more sophisticated neurosymbolic planning and learning integrations accounting for task stochasticity. One option is to exploit learned logical specifications for the efficient guidance of a probabilistically optimal planner (Meli et al, 2024). Alternatively, we could exploit our recent results in neurosymbolic DRL, to simultaneously learn a stochastic DRL policy enhanced by online refined ASP heuristics (Veronese et al, 2024, in publication). In terms of safety guarantees on the overall execution (currently yielded from the deterministic reasoning approach under expert supervision), they shall be then provided via stochastic formal verification (Marzari et al, 2024) or shielding techniques (Mazzi et al, 2023a).

User validation

Our work represents a preliminary architecture for interpretable human-robot interaction, where the human plays the role of a teacher and supervisor for the student robotic system. Application to more complex tasks and real scenarios with physical robots will require an extended user study to assess the actual benefits of human-robot inter-play (Fosch-Villaronga et al, 2023), and the implementation of more sophisticated and user-oriented communication interfaces (Long et al, 2023), e.g., implementing voice commands with automatic speech-to-text and text-to-speech translation in the online refinement phase.

7 Conclusion

In this paper, we have proposed a methodology based on ILP and ASP to discover task specifications, encoding action preconditions, constraints and effects, from raw video-kinematic datasets of robotic executions. Our approach leverages on any unsupervised action identification algorithm to retrieve ILP examples from recordings, combining them with almost task-agnostic commonsense concepts defined by an user, in order to increase the interpretability, trustability and social acceptance of learned axioms.

In the context of the peg transfer task with dual-arm dVRK, a benchmark training exercise for novice surgeons, we show that our offline learning pipeline requires very basic commonsense concepts, which are often task-agnostic since they only incorporate information about the location of robotic arms with respect to the environment, and the kinematic state of the grippers. Moreover, the online learning algorithm is able to refine task knowledge even with few task examples.

This work represents an important step towards interpretable robotic task learning and generalization from limited raw recordings of execution, showing promising results for the scalability of our methodology to more complex and challenging robotic scenarios.

8.1 Unsupervised learning of ASP task knowledge

8.1.1 As​e​mA_{sem}
release(V1,t) :- not reachable(V1,peg,V2,t),not reachable(V1,ring,V2),
    closed_gripper(V1,t),placed(ring,V2,peg,V3,t).
grasp(V1,ring,V,t) :- not closed_gripper(V1,t),at(V1,ring,V2,t).

    reachable(V3,peg,V2,t),V3!=V1.
extract(V1,ring,V2,t) :- closed_gripper(V1,t),placed(ring,V2,peg,V3,t),

terminated(at(V1,peg,V2),t+1) :- move(V1,center,V3,t),color(V2).
initiated(at(A,peg,C),t+1) :- move(A,peg,C,t).
terminated(at(V1,ring,V2),t+1) :- move(V1,peg,V3,t),color(V2).
initiated(at(V1,ring,V2),t+1) :- move(V1,ring,V2,t).

initiated(at(V1,center),t+1) :- move(V1,center,V2,t).

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
